overview: The Maitrakas ruled from Valabhi in western India from roughly the fifth to the eighth century. Their kingdom supported trade, religious institutions and celebrated learning. The map’s 700 to 800 span selects its late phase; its broad western Indian polygon is an approximate outline, not proof of a fixed frontier.

periods.title: Earlier dynastic growth
periods.summary: A ruling family centred on Valabhi established authority in Gujarat, especially Kathiawar.

periods.title: Learning and urban wealth
periods.summary: Xuanzang described a prosperous country, religious establishments and scholars whose works circulated widely.

periods.title: Late grants and uncertain collapse
periods.summary: Later charters came from military camps. Grants continued into the 760s; the circumstances of the dynasty’s final fall remain disputed.

items.text: A sixth-century charter remembers Bhatakka and Dharasena as generals, then Dronasimha as a maharaja, or great king. The family’s own account connected military service with growing royal rank. Its extravagant battle praise is also a reminder that rulers helped write their reputations.

Dhruvasena I’s order addressed officials, watch-station officers, soldiers and other people responsible for administration. A grant needed more than a king’s announcement: the people collecting dues and enforcing authority also had to recognize it.

That grant names village holdings and irrigation works, gives land to two Brahmins, and provides for their descendants. It invokes merit for the king’s parents. Family remembrance, religious practice and the control of productive land meet in one legal document.

Xuanzang described Valabhi as a place where rare goods arrived from distant regions and some families possessed enormous wealth. He also connected the subordinate region of Suratta with sea commerce. These are a seventh-century traveler’s impressions of prosperous commercial connections.

A grant of 609 provided for monks’ clothing, meals, beds or seats, and medicines for sick members of the community. Care had an economic foundation: endowments were intended to keep supplies coming. The document does not identify a particular treatment or describe a public hospital.

In 605, Shiladitya I supported the Dudda monastery with a village, three fields, two irrigation cisterns and four wells with flower gardens. The wells and gardens lay within Valabhi’s territory. Water helped sustain both productive land and the flowers used in worship.

The 609 grant also budgeted for repairing cracked or damaged monastery buildings and supplying flowers, incense and lamp oil for worship. A religious establishment needed a maintenance plan. Even a grand sacred building could develop an unglamorous crack.

Shiladitya I’s official religious title expressed devotion to Shiva, yet he funded Buddhist communities. His successors continued such grants. Personal worship and royal patronage could reach different religious groups, making the kingdom’s institutional life more varied than a single royal title suggests.

Xuanzang reported an annual seven-day royal assembly at which monks received food, robes and medicine. Public giving joined royal display with practical provision. His account is a witness to court-supported religious hospitality, rather than a menu for every family in Valabhi.

The noblewoman Dudda founded a monastery for monks. Merchants, learned monks and senior officials also established Buddhist institutions. Royal grants often maintained foundations created by somebody else: the king was not the only person who could organize a lasting institution.

Valabhi also contained nunneries with their own economic resources. Copper plates preserve royal support for these women’s communities. Such records add organized female religious life to a historical picture that would otherwise be dominated by kings and male travelers.

Xuanzang associated a monastery near the city with Gunamati and Sthiramati, scholars who composed widely circulated works. Valabhi’s importance rested partly on ideas that could travel beyond its walls. His description concerns advanced religious scholarship, not universal elementary schooling.

A grooved shell-bangle fragment from Vallabhipur, catalogued as Maitraka, was carefully cut and polished. It is a small surviving piece of personal adornment. Someone valued a smooth finish even on an object far less grand than a royal monument.

Another excavated ornament is a pale stone bead, smoothed on the outside and pierced through the centre. The tiny hole allowed it to be threaded. This modest object preserves the patient shaping and drilling that lay behind a finished piece of jewellery.

Excavations reported in 2026 exposed burnt-brick walls at Darbargarh and mud-brick as well as fired-brick remains near Mafat Nagar. ASI officials provisionally placed recovered material within the fifth to eighth centuries. These discoveries are gradually adding actual buildings to the city known from documents.

The same excavation season recovered gaming pieces alongside coins, seals and ornaments. Games belong in the picture of this busy settlement too. The preliminary report does not identify the rules, so we cannot yet challenge a Maitraka player to a properly reconstructed match.

Most complete Maitraka charters consist of two copper plates, held together by rings. A seal showing a bull helped authenticate the document. These durable title deeds were designed to preserve rights: important paperwork could be distinctly heavier than a sheet of paper.

Written Sanskrit: “स्वस्ति वलभीतः” (svasti valabhītaḥ), “Hail! From Valabhī.” This greeting opens Dhruvasena I’s Palitana plates, dated Valabhi year 206 in the sixth century. The words are shown in modern Devanagari type, not the original engraved letter shapes; this witness predates the map’s 700 start.

ending.text: Maitraka grants continued into 765 or 766. Invasions in the later eighth century probably ended the dynasty, but the sequence and date of Valabhi’s destruction are uncertain. The imported 800 endpoint should not be read as an exact fall date or the disappearance of the region’s inhabitants.
